newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec premier calls for reduced government role.
newsitem.headline: Quebec premier calls for reduced government role.

text.p: Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard called for reducing the government's role in society at a conference on Tuesday as protesters representing the poor, unemployed and students picketed outside the meeting's venue.

"Quebec has achieved economic maturity. It no longer needs the State to do everything," Bouchard told a blue-ribbon gathering of business, union and community leaders at his Summit Conference on the Economy and Employment.
Bouchard's remarks were a departure from the usual social democratic values of his Parti Quebecois government.

Picketers opposed to the separatist premier's budget austerity measures made bonfires of their placards in the street, burned Bouchard in effigy and threw burning placards at riot police. But they dispersed soon after the premier's spoke.
Bouchard pressed on with his clarion call to Quebec society in his speech.

"We know that we are too deeply in debt and too heavily taxed. We know that we spend proportionally more on public services than most industrialised societies, including the social-democratic countries of Europe," Bouchard said in his keynote address opening the three-day conference.

Participants in the summit, including the heads of major Quebec corporations such as Bombardier Inc, Imasco Ltd and Royal Bank of Canada, will discuss proposals to revive the provincial economy, create more jobs and balance the government books.
In his speech, Bouchard said Quebec business must adjust to new economic realities, abandoning reliance on protectionism, free-flowing subsidies and monopolies.
Bouchard said all of Quebec society must become more competitve, focussing on the prime objective of creating jobs to reduce the province's 12.6 percent unemployment rate.

Ghislain Dufour, head of Quebec's largest employer group, told Reuters after the speech he hoped Bouchard's government would take concrete measures such as reducing payroll costs and regulation to help business revive the economy.

Dufour said that after two years in power, during which it fought and lost a bitterly fought referendum on sovereignty, it was time for the Parti Quebecois government to implement appropriate economic policy.
"We cannot be constantly waiting for action," Dufour said.

Laurent Beaudoin, chairman and chief executive of aerospace and transportation equipment maker Bombardier, said Bouchard appeared willing to discuss ways to give the corporate sector more flexibility to manage its affairs.
"He showed much more openness regarding what we should be doing with the economy," Bouchard said.

Beaudoin, one of the few major Quebec business leaders to speak publicly against separation during the referendum campaign, said he was also impressed that Bouchard reached out to the province's English-speaking minority in his speech.

Daniel Johnson, head of the Liberal Party of Quebec, which sits in opposition in the provincial parliament, said Bouchard must acknowledge that his government's separatist political program was hurting the economy.
"The premier should really change his tune," Johnson said.
